name: Fatima Alvarez
think: Robots by 2034 give her **seven more years** of wages.
She admits she'd be **tempted to coast** for most of that time.
privateAnswer: Robots by 2034 means I'm 35. That's better and worse. Better because I get seven more years of wages, worse because I'd be tempted to do nothing for six of them, and I know myself.

name: Marco Gupta
think: Five years is enough to earn a **maintenance ticket** if I start now.
My press work likely lasts until **about 2034**.
privateAnswer: I think five years is enough to get a proper ticket in maintenance, if I start now. The thinking side arrives in 2031, so the planning jobs I could never get go first. My bit on the presses probably lasts till about 2034, which gives me a window.

name: Uma Nakamura
think: Five years lets me make **two jumps**: programming, then robot maintenance.
I'm used to **learning fast**, so the race feels winnable.
privateAnswer: I think five years lets me ride the wave a bit. I could learn programming now and use it for three or four years, then move into robot maintenance before 2034. It's two jumps instead of one, but I'm used to learning fast.

name: Colin Schmidt
think: It's the **same end**, just later, around 2034.
I might save a bit and **see where jobs go**.
privateAnswer: Deep down, it's the same as the fast one, just later. I'd be 32 when the robots get good, and I still don't fancy my chances learning computers. But five years might be enough to save a bit and see where the jobs are going.

name: Dana Ziegler
think: Five years lets me climb **one rung** to engineering support.
That work might last until **2034** or a bit after.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think five years gives me time to get one rung up. If I can get to engineering support by 2031, I'm on the people who fix the robots, not the people they replace. That might last until 2034 or a bit after.

name: Karl Fischer
think: Bend programming pays off **until about 2031**, then it fades.
I'd want to move into **robot maintenance** before 2034.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years is enough to earn a bit from the in-between stuff. Learning bend programming now pays off until about 2031. After that, I'd want to be in robot maintenance before 2034.

name: Sara Mensah
think: Five years gives time for **care work**, which needs a human hand.
Kofi may need a **new job** with his hands.
privateAnswer: I think five years gives me time to get something a robot can't do so quickly, like caring for old folk. I don't like change, but I know old people want a human hand. Kofi might need a new job too, maybe something with his hands.

name: Aaron Rossi
think: I can get a **maintenance qualification** before robots arrive in 2034.
Gina has time to switch to **dental nursing** before 2031.
privateAnswer: I think five years lets me get a maintenance qualification before the robots come in 2034. Gina has time to move into dental nursing before 2031. It's tight, but it's a plan.

name: Beth Young
think: Five years allows a **two-step plan**: programming, then maintenance.
My partner Tom has time to finish his **carpentry apprenticeship** too.
privateAnswer: I think five years lets me use robot programming for a few years, then move into maintenance before 2034. It's a two-step plan, and I like a plan. Tom has time to finish his apprenticeship.

name: Ivan Evans
think: I think I'd finally get **good at the job** just as it's taken away.
Eight years to the robots is most of my **working life** before forty.
privateAnswer: Eight years until the robots arrive, and I'd finally learn the press properly just in time for a robot to take the press off me. That's the cruel bit. I'd have time to get the warning off my name, and I'd still be under forty when it's gone.

name: Priya Larsen
think: Privately, robots on the line by **2034** leaves me a real window.
Being about **thirty-five** then feels young enough to change trades.
privateAnswer: Privately I think five years plus three more for robots is a real window. That's 2034 for the line, so I'd be about thirty-five. It's enough time to get qualified if I don't waste it.

name: Yusuf Rahman
think: Privately, robots by **2034** gives me about eight years to become the fixer.
Being **adaptive**, I'd rather arrive early than late.
privateAnswer: Off the record, five years is good for me. Robots on the line by 2034 gives me about eight years in total, long enough to become the person who installs and fixes them. I'm adaptive, so I'd rather be early to that than late.

name: Freya Weber
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still push me out of the wrapper job in my thirties.
I'm **not good at learning** new things, so the extra time may not help.
privateAnswer: Honestly, five years sounds like a lot, but robots by 2034 still means I'm out of the wrapper job in my thirties. I'd have time, but I wouldn't know where to start.

name: Gareth Diaz
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still take the press job.
Five years is time to **get a trade** while I'm around thirty-five.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 still take the press job, but five years gives me time to get a trade. I'd be about thirty-five, still young enough to start somewhere new. It's scary, but I can see a path.

name: Nora Khan
think: Privately, robots by **2034** gives me time to become a technician and more.
At about **thirty-five**, I'd still be early in a new career.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 gives me enough time to become a technician and then something more, maybe a robot service engineer. I'd be about thirty-five, still early. I think I'd be all right if I keep moving.

name: Victor Petrov
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still take my job.
Having a family and **no work** at thirty-two is my fear.
privateAnswer: Honestly, robots by 2034 still take my job, but by then I could have a trade. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe a baby on the way. That's what scares me, having a family and no work.

name: Daria Wagner
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still take the knitting.
Mark would be **qualified** by then, and I'd have time for care work.
privateAnswer: Honestly, robots by 2034 still take the knitting, but by then Mark would be a qualified plumber, and I'd have time to get a care qualification. I'd be about thirty-five. It's frightening, but I can see us getting through.

name: Emeka Chen
think: Privately, robots by **2034** let me grow the workshop slowly.
By 2031 I'd want benches paying **half my rent**.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 means I can stay at Brookfield a few more years and grow the workshop on the side. By 2031 I'd want the benches paying half my rent. I like this version.

name: Lena Ito
think: The **2031 AI** won't touch my shift, but the **2034 robots** will.
At **35** I'd be old to start again, but not too old.
privateAnswer: I think five years is long enough for me to feel guilty for doing nothing. The AI in 2031 won't touch my shift, but by 2034 the robots will. I'd be 35 then, which is old to start again but not too old.

name: Tomas Olsen
think: Five years matches **my speed**: watch the first robot cells, then follow.
The 2031 AI hits the office; the **2034 robots** hit me.
privateAnswer: Honestly, five years is just about my speed. I'd watch the first plants put in robot cells, see what jobs come out of it, and follow. The AI arriving in 2031 hits the office, and the robots in 2034 hit me.

name: Bianca Usman
think: Five years is **enough** for me to qualify and fix robots for a while.
My partner has until **2031** to move into hands-on or AI-managing work.
privateAnswer: I think five years is enough for me. I'd be a qualified technician by 2029 and have a few years fixing robots before they get really good. Kofi's job hits in 2031, so he's got time to move into something hands-on or something that manages the AI.

name: Carlos Baker
think: With five years, I'd probably **drift** and stay on the press until 2033.
I'd only move when I see the **robot** in the building, which is probably a mistake.
privateAnswer: I think five years means I'd probably drift. I'd stay on the press until 2033 because it pays well, and only move when I see the robot in the building. That's probably a mistake, but that's me.

name: Jade Hansen
think: The **2034 robots** hit us, but I could be a qualified electrician by then.
With my partner helping, we'd have done it **properly**.
privateAnswer: I think five years suits me. The AI in 2031 hits the office, the robots in 2034 hit us, and by then I could be qualified as an electrician. Sam would help, and we'd have done it properly.

name: Rafael Novak
think: Five years lets me take the **technician job** and build the bikes on the side.
When AGI arrives in **2031**, I'd switch to bikes full time.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years gives me time to do both. I can get the technician job, earn more for a few years, and build the bike business on the side. When AGI arrives in 2031 I'd switch over to the bikes full time.

name: Zoe Tanaka
think: Five years is enough to have a **child** and get settled first.
I've never done anything else, so I'd worry about **after 2034**.
privateAnswer: I think five years is enough for us to have a child and get settled. The robots come in 2034, so I'd probably keep my job until then. I've never done anything but weaving, so I'd worry about what I'd do after the robots come.

name: Adam Abbott
think: Five years is about **right** for me to switch before robots arrive.
I'd already be **out** of the factory when robots come in 2034.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years is about right for me. I'd keep the router job until about 2032, get married as planned, and build up the fitting work on the side. When robots come to the factory in 2034, I'd already be out.

name: Hana Gupta
think: Five years is **workable**: quality first, then maintenance around 2030.
By **2034** I'd have two skills, and medicine may be slower still.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years is workable. I could get the quality certificate, use it for a few years, and then switch to maintenance around 2030. The robots come in 2034, maybe later in medicine, and by then I'd have two skills.

name: Omar Moreau
think: I think five years only buys **more of the same** before the same ending.
I think I'd be **35** with no other trade when the robots come.
privateAnswer: Really, I think it buys me a few more years of the same job and then the same ending. The planning side of the plant goes in 2031, the presses go around 2034, and I'm 35 with nothing else. Five years is better than two, but it's still not my life sorted.

name: Wendy Schmidt
think: I think I'd still **lose the operator job**, just later.
I think eight years is enough to become the person who **fixes the robots**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd still lose the operator job, just later. But eight years before the robots is enough time to become the person who fixes them, if I'm smart about it. It still worries me, because fitters might not be safe forever either.

name: Erik Zhang
think: I think five years gets me **qualified** as a robot technician.
I think **Jun's wage** as a nurse would change everything for us.
privateAnswer: Honestly, five years is long enough to get qualified as a robot technician and get a few years of better pay before the end. Jun would be a qualified nurse by then, so we'd have two incomes. That changes a lot for me.

name: Fatima Fischer
think: I think I'd still be **out of the bakery** by 2034.
I think it's the **same ending**, just slower, with Jonas going first.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd still be out of the bakery by 2034, just a bit later. Jonas would go first again, in 2031. It's slower, but it's the same ending for us.

name: Marco Lopez
think: I think I'd still **lose the die-cutter** job, just later.
I think 35 with an **electrician's ticket** beats 32 with nothing.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd still lose the die-cutter job, but later, and I'd have time to get a trade. I'd be 35 with an electrician's ticket, which is better than 32 with nothing. It still worries me.

name: Uma Rossi
think: I think five years is enough to become a **line technician**.
I think it's **tight but doable** before robots arrive.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think five years is enough to become a line technician, earn more and save. Then I'd move into robot maintenance before the robots arrive. It's tight but doable.

name: Colin Yilmaz
think: I think five years **helps a bit** with wages and savings.
I think I'd still be **out by 2034**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, it helps a bit. I'd have a few more years of wages and maybe save something after the wedding. But I'd still be out by 2034.

name: Dana Evans
think: I think I'd still **lose the cannery job** eventually.
I think five years lets me **save and train** in the evenings.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd still lose the cannery job eventually. But five years means I can save and train in the evenings.

name: Karl Kowalski
think: I think five years lets me become a **robot technician**.
I think I'd still be **worried** about the end.
privateAnswer: Off the record, five years lets me become a robot technician and earn more for a few years. I'd still be worried about the end, but I'd be better off.

name: Sara Rahman
think: I think robots by 2034 give me about **seven years** at the machines.
I'm afraid I'll **wait too long** because I hate changing.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 means I've got about seven years at the machines. That's long enough to get somewhere else, if I actually move. The trouble is, I know me, I'll wait until it's too late, because I hate changing.

name: Aaron Walsh
think: I think I have about **eight years** before the lathes stop needing me.
I'd **copy** whoever adapts well, because I'm second, not first.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd have about eight years before the lathes don't need me. That's enough to see who's doing well and copy them, which is my usual way. I'm not first, I'm second, and second is fine.

name: Beth Diaz
think: I think robots by 2034 give me time to become an **engineer**.
I'm a **hands person**, so the three-year gap protects me.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'd be well placed. Robots by 2034 gives me time to finish the apprenticeship, get a few years as an engineer and maybe move to the installer side. The thinking part of my job goes in 2031, but I'm not a thinking-job person anyway.

name: Ivan Jensen
think: I think robots by 2034 give me about **eight years**.
Six years at the plant **flew by**, so eight will too.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 gives me eight years, more or less. That's a long time to me, but I know it goes, I've been at the plant six years already and it feels like nothing. I'd still end up out of a job I like.

name: Priya Petrov
think: I think I'd be on the line until about **thirty-five**.
The **team leader** job is shaky, because scheduling goes in 2031.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 means I'd be on the line until I'm about thirty-five. That's long enough to save and move. But the thinking parts of the job, the scheduling and the quality sign-off, go in 2031, so the team leader job I want is shaky.

name: Yusuf Varga
think: I think I'd go from **process technician** to robot commissioning.
By 2034 I'd be **thirty-five** with rare skills.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd have time to be the process technician for a few years and then move to robot commissioning. By 2034 I'd be thirty-five, with skills nobody at the plant has today.

name: Freya Chen
think: I think I have about **eight years** at the tufting machines.
Watching it come is **almost worse** for someone slow with change.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots by 2034 means I've got about eight years at the tufting machines. It's still my job going. I'm not good with new things, so eight years of watching it come is almost worse.

name: Gareth Ibrahim
think: Robots by **2034** give me seven more years at the press, until I'm 34.
I can't tell whether **electricians** will still be needed after the robots arrive.
privateAnswer: Truth is, robots by 2034 gives me seven years at the press, and I'd be 34. That's enough to get the electrician qualification properly and work a couple of years at it. Whether electricians last after that, I honestly don't know.

name: Nora Olsen
think: Robots by **2034** leave a few golden years for technicians installing them everywhere.
After installation a plant needs **one technician** where it had ten operators.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this one. Robots by 2034 means seven years on the floor, and a few years in the middle as a technician, when every plant is installing robots and nobody knows how. That's the gold rush, and I'd want to be there with a toolbox.

name: Victor Torres
think: I get about **eight years**, because robots reach the floor around 2034.
That's enough to **pay down** a flat but not to escape the end.
privateAnswer: For me it means about eight years, because the robots for the floor come around 2034. I'd be thirty-five. That's long enough to get the flat and pay a chunk of it off, and still be in trouble at the end.

name: Daria Baker
think: I'd have about **eight years** before robots can do the moulding.
That's enough to learn a **new skill** properly, but I won't be loading moulds at 35.
privateAnswer: For me it means about eight years before robots can do the moulding, so around 2034. That's long enough to get a new skill properly, not in a panic. Still, I don't think I'm loading moulds at thirty-five.

name: Emeka Haddad
think: About **eight years** before robots reach my floor gives me a real stretch.
I can work as a **robot technician** for years and save hard.
privateAnswer: Privately, it's better for me. Robots on the floor around 2034 gives me about eight years. I can be a robot technician for a good stretch and save hard.

name: Lena Novak
think: Robots on the presses around **2034** gives me about eight more years.
That's enough to **save more**, not enough to stop worrying.
privateAnswer: Privately, robots on the presses around 2034 means about eight more years for me. I'd be thirty-five. Enough to save a lot more, not enough to stop worrying.

name: Tomas Silva
think: I'd have about **eight years** on the line, until 2034.
Ana's job goes earlier, maybe **2031**.
That's enough to sort things out, but **not to relax**.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd have until about 2034 on the line, so around eight years. Ana's job goes earlier, maybe 2031. That's enough time to sort things out, but not enough to relax.

name: Bianca Abbott
think: I'd have about **eight years**, until 2034.
That's enough to move into **setting up robots**, not just running machines.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd have about eight years, until 2034. That's enough to move up and into setting up the robots, not just running machines. Kofi would have five years to switch.

name: Carlos Garcia
think: The **thinking AI** in 2031 barely touches my hands-on job.
Robots in 2034 would hit me at **thirty-five**, young enough but unwelcome.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, the thinking AI in 2031 hardly touches me, I don't do much of that. The robots in 2034 do, and I'd be thirty-five. That's young enough to start again, but old enough that I'd hate it.

name: Jade Moreau
think: The **paperwork** goes in 2031, but the hands-on side lasts until 2034.
Five years is enough to become **the person who fixes** the machines.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd think my operator job lasts until around 2034, when the robots come. The thinking parts go in 2031, so the paperwork side goes first, but the hands-on side gives me three more years. Five years is enough time to become the person who fixes the machines, if I start soon.

name: Rafael Santos
think: My shop can survive if it's **early**, and I could run its robots.
Robots in 2034 still need someone to **set up fixtures** for a while.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd think my shop could survive if it's early, and I could be the guy who runs its robots. AGI in 2031 takes the programming, but robots in 2034 still need someone on the floor to set up fixtures and sort out problems for a while. Five years is long enough to become that person at my own shop.

name: Zoe Zhang
think: She worries she'd **wait too long**, telling herself there's still time.
Watching the **planner's job** go in 2031 would be her warning sign.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years scares me in a different way, because I'd be tempted to wait. I know myself. I'd tell myself there's still time and then it's 2033. The thinking AI would take Karen's planning job in 2031, and I'd watch that and still be standing at press four.

name: Adam Farah
think: Five years is his **sweet spot** to move, once others go first.
**Robot maintenance** looks like the job that lasts longest.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think five years is my sweet spot to move, if I see others move first. By 2031 the programming's gone, so I'd want to be on the maintenance side by then, fixing the robots that come in 2034. That's the job that lasts longest, I reckon.

name: Hana Lopez
think: Five years is enough for the **automation diploma**.
By 2031 thinking AI changes repairs, so the training may be **half gone**.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years is enough for me to get a proper qualification, maybe the two-year automation diploma. But the thinking AI arrives in 2031, and that changes how robots get fixed too. I'd be training for a job that's half gone by the time I finish.

name: Omar Reyes
think: He knows he'd **wait too long**, hoping orders return.
Once the office empties in **2031**, he'd have only three years left.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, I'd wait too long. I know I would. Five years sounds like a lot when you're stamping brackets, and I'd keep thinking the orders would come back. Then 2031 comes, the office empties, and I'd only have three years left.

name: Wendy Yilmaz
think: Five years gives her room for **one more skill**.
With the knitting room safe until **2034**, she has seven years.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think five years gives me room to get one more skill. The thinking AI in 2031 hits Holm's office first, and the knitting room has until 2034. That's seven years for me. Enough to get a certificate, not enough to waste time.

name: Erik Dubois
think: Five years is **close to perfect** for an automation qualification.
Tallis could **close early** if the owners build a robot plant elsewhere.
privateAnswer: Privately, five years is close to perfect for me. I'd have time to get a proper automation qualification and save a bit. By 2031 the thinking AI arrives, and I'd want to already be the person who knows how to run AI on a factory floor. Then I'd have three more years before the robots.

name: Fatima Kowalski
think: She'd **do too little**, because she dislikes change.
Her fiancé **Piotr** would have to sit her down and push her to act.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd probably do too little, because I don't like change. I'd keep baking until 2031 and then say there are still three years. That's how I am. Piotr would push me.

name: Marco Quinn
think: Five years lets him finish an **electrical qualification** by 2030.
He'd still have **three hands-on years** at Ashby, but wants others to go first.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think five years is about right for me. It's enough to finish an electrical qualification by 2030, before the thinking AI comes, and I'd still have three years of hands-on work at Ashby while I get going. I'd want to see one or two others do it first, though.

name: Uma Walsh
think: **Routine** operating hours remain at risk, but time helps.
**Funding**, paid study days and a posted nearby job must all line up.
privateAnswer: I still see a big threat to routine operating hours, but I can build a real qualification while drawing wages. An unpaid maintenance course would take the rent money I need before any robot takes my shift.

name: Colin Costa
think: Everything I'm good at is **hands-on**, which is exactly what robots take by **2034**.
There's time to get ahead of it, but I **don't know where** to go.
privateAnswer: Privately, eight years until a robot does my job is enough time to get out ahead of it, but I don't really know where to go. Everything I'm good at is hands-on. If it's all robots by 2034, the hands-on stuff is exactly what goes.

name: Dana Jensen
think: I'd probably be fine if I **move within** two or three years.
Robots need fixers, but **far fewer** than the operators they replace.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd think I'd probably be okay if I move in the next two or three years. The trouble is the robots that replace operators will need people to fix them, but nowhere near as many of us.

name: Karl Patel
think: Five years is enough to **build something** as an owner.
Owning a robot shop is both **progressive and selfish**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think five years is enough for me to build something. If I can run a small robot shop with a couple of mates, we're owners, not employees. That's the progressive bit and the selfish bit at the same time.

name: Sara Varga
think: I expect **Northgate** to close before 2034.
I'd be about **34** with a trade that no longer exists.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think Northgate closes before 2034. An old plant with an old corrugator, and a new robot plant somewhere cheaper. I'd be about 34 and out of work in a trade that doesn't exist anymore.

name: Aaron Bauer
think: I'd still buy a **modest flat** with seven years of wages.
My worry is **too many people** crowding into the same trades.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think I'd still buy the flat, but a modest one. Seven years of wages is a long time to save and plan. My worry is that everybody piles into the same trades and there's too many plumbers by 2034.

name: Beth Ibrahim
think: I can get into **robotics** before 2034 easily.
My partner Hassan **puts things off**, which worries me.
Hassan has until **2031**, enough to retrain if he starts early.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I can get into robotics before 2034 easily. I'd still be a bit worried, mostly because my partner Hassan tends to put things off. He has until 2031, which is enough for him to retrain if he starts early.

name: Ivan Okafor
think: I'd last until about **34** on the panel line.
That's enough time to learn **joinery** with my uncle.
I know I'm **not good at change**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think I'd get to about 34 on the panel line. That's enough time to learn joinery properly and maybe go into business with my uncle. But I'm not good at change, and I know that about myself.

name: Priya Torres
think: I've got **a good few years** at the looms.
I'd have children and train in **loom maintenance** before 2034.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think I've got a good few years at the looms. I'd have my children, go back part-time, and train for loom maintenance before 2034. It still worries me, but there's time.

name: Yusuf Alvarez
think: **Automation** still threatens routine hours, but preparation can precede it.
**Paid** training and a real local vacancy matter more than a certificate by itself.
privateAnswer: I expect mould loading and routine checks to shrink eventually, but I could save and qualify before they do. The local toolrooms may also change, so I would want a posted vacancy rather than faith that every factory will hire.

name: Freya Haddad
think: At **35**, I still need years of factory wages despite a larger reserve.
Five more years let me **save and train**, subject to real paid places and vacancies.
privateAnswer: I would be 35 when those robots arrive. Five years of senior pay could build the reserve further, but I would still need a wage for years after that. I can prepare without pretending a qualification guarantees a vacancy.

name: Gareth Nakamura
think: At **35**, I can gain a second skill while earning a lead wage.
A **certificate** matters only with a posted safe local job and enough pay.
privateAnswer: I would be 35 when the capable robots reach the floor. I could build a second skill while earning the lead wage, but a job with the same title might pay less. We still hope to buy the flat, so I cannot treat training as a guarantee of income.

name: Nora Silva
think: Maintenance could become a **durable role** if a real local post pays fairly.
A **technical diploma** and course do not guarantee a vacancy.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty two at the thinking date and thirty five when robots can handle the press work. With more warning I could move toward machine maintenance, but I would still need a posted job at a fair rate, not a certificate in a drawer.

name: Victor Ziegler
think: The **2034 robot date** gives me years of corrugator wages, but no lifetime guarantee.
Our **flat and savings** cannot fund a long career without paid work.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty two when office thinking work changes and thirty five when the physical line is at risk. The good wage, flat and savings help me wait, but I cannot live on them until old age.

name: Daria Garcia
think: A proper **controls course** could move me into maintenance.
A new **job title** is useless without a posted opening at bill-covering pay.
privateAnswer: I could qualify for maintenance while the line still needs me, but only if the course teaches actual controls and safe isolation. I would not leave a good wage for a maintenance title without a posted opening at workable pay.

name: Emeka Mensah
think: A practical **controls skill** could protect my earnings.
A **certificate** without a real local commissioning opening would not protect my operator wage.
privateAnswer: I have time to turn the diploma into a commissioning skill, but only if real machines and experienced engineers are part of the training. A certificate without an opening would not protect my wage.

name: Lena Santos
think: Good **current wages** can strengthen our deposit before robots arrive.
A **maintenance certificate** only helps if a real comparable-pay job is posted.
privateAnswer: I would be thirty two when plans change and thirty five when the press itself is at risk. A few years of good wages could strengthen the deposit, but I still do not want to train for a role that has no posted job.

name: Tomas Young
think: Current **hot-end wages** help me prepare, but the post-2034 role is uncertain.
A **maintenance course** needs practical instruction and a real paid opening.
privateAnswer: I can keep earning on the hot end during the warning, but that does not settle what work pays after 2034. A plant maintenance role would fit my diploma only with practical instruction and a posted vacancy.

name: Bianca Farah
